source.title: Guiding Data Collection via Factored Scaling Curves
source.authors: Li-Han Zha; Apurva Badithela; Michael Zhang; Justin Lidard; Jeremy Bao; Emily Zhou; David Snyder; Allen Z. Ren; Dhruv Shah; Anirudha Majumdar

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law-shaped performance curves in robotic imitation learning, a different training regime and performance measure from language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study fits power laws to robotic policy performance as demonstration counts vary and reports qualitative extrapolation results. It cites language-model scaling laws as related work but does not test language-model loss scaling. Data-allocation success-rate comparisons are not included as rows because they evaluate allocation strategies rather than the power-law form itself.
record.test_reason: Mainly a data-collection method paper that assumes a power-law form, 1−a(n+c)^b, for robot-policy success rate versus demonstration count. Section 4.2 does check the fitted curves' extrapolations against held-out added-data results for π0 fine-tuning, which bears weakly on V5 (power-law form in a new training regime). The evidence is figure-only and qualitative, and the data range is under one order of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that factored scaling curves can be reliably extrapolated to predict how policy success changes with added factor-specific data, and use this to guide data collection (up to 26% over baselines). They note that large-budget extrapolation is less precise, and that real-success curves are marginally more predictive than the embedding proxy.
record.recipe_differences: Fits performance-versus-demonstration-count curves for robotic imitation policies, not held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens, or training compute; evaluates factor-specific curves and data allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Curve construction and data-allocation choices affect outcomes; an outlier can distort a fit, and large-budget extrapolation is reported as less precise. The paper also compares one-factor, pairwise, and grouped curves, and proxy embedding choices.

fits_no_version.finding: FSC-guided data allocation beats Equal/Greedy/Re-Mix baselines by up to 26% success rate (Tables 1–4, Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law-based per-factor scaling curves can guide robot data collection better than heuristic allocation.

record.problems: Real-world evaluations use relatively few trials per policy (12 for Fold Towel, 18 for Mouse in Drawer, and 20 for Pick Place); the authors note evaluation noise and reduced precision at large budgets. The reported curve-prediction results are qualitative rather than accompanied by numerical prediction errors or uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude (the range is ~0–160 extra demos). Loss as the measure (only success rate or partial credit is used). Comparison of power-law against alternative functional forms. Image/video models, repeated data, and transfer scaling.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested for language models; robot extrapolation spans under one order of magnitude.

missing.what: Fitted power-law parameters and held-out test points for the simulation tasks. Several exponents are near −0.01 (nearly flat or linear), while others are around −0.6 to −0.7. These figures show how well the form fits beyond the fit range.
With a 300-demo initial dataset, performance has already saturated and FSC gains vanish.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law form is assumed, not tested against alternatives. Fits use as few as four points over a range well under one order of magnitude, with very few real-world evaluation trials. Some fitted exponents (~−0.01) make the curve almost indistinguishable from linear. Weight the V5 support accordingly; an alternative reading would classify this as uses_without_test/T4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Reports extrapolation in robotics, but not prediction of language-model loss on runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not measure compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
Does not compare model depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests demonstration-count scaling of robotic policy performance, including π0 fine-tuning; does not test image/video generative models, repeated-data training, or transfer beyond the robotic settings studied.
Does not test language-model downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Does not test language-model exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices. Its observations about robotics curve fitting do not establish that published language-model laws disagree.

rows.subject: π0
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned; only the action expert is trained
rows.operation_detail: Fit a factored power-law curve to policy success rate versus demonstration count, then compare its extrapolation with added-data results.
rows.measure: Agreement between predicted and actual policy success rate after adding factor data
rows.value: figure only; the text says the extrapolation matches actual performance almost perfectly
rows.note: The textual description supports the figure-only values and says the larger-count extrapolation matched closely.
rows.check: Value is figure-only; the text says the extrapolation matches 'almost perfectly'. The fit uses n=0–60 and is tested at n=80/160, well under an order of magnitude. The measure is success rate, not loss.

rows.subject: π0
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned; only the action expert is trained
rows.operation_detail: Fit a factored power-law curve to policy success rate versus demonstration count and compare its extrapolation with added-data results.
rows.measure: Agreement between predicted and actual policy success-rate change after adding factor data
rows.value: figure only; the text says the change in success rate was exactly as predicted
rows.note: The paper gives a qualitative account of the curve’s extrapolation accuracy.
rows.check: Figure-only; the text says success improved 'exactly as predicted'. No numeric error is given, and the evaluation has only ~12 trials per policy.

rows.subject: π0
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned; only the action expert is trained
rows.operation_detail: Fit and extrapolate factored performance curves for the factor groups.

conditions.value: An outlier at n=60 distorts the fit

rows.value: The outlier slightly distorts the fit, but FSC still selects the right factor
rows.note: The text reports a fit disturbance but does not give a numeric prediction error.
rows.check: The text describes an outlier at n=60 that 'slightly distorts the fit'. The measure mixes fit quality with whether FSC picks the right factor; factor selection is the method's outcome, not the power-law form.

rows.subject: Diffusion Policy
rows.operation_detail: Fit factored performance curves and extrapolate to larger additional-data budgets.
rows.measure: Precision of policy-performance extrapolation at large data budgets
rows.value: The authors state that predictions at large K can be less precise; they identify K=500 results as affected by saturation and substantial evaluation noise
rows.locator: Limitations and Future Work; Appendix A.4, Table 7
rows.note: The paper does not report a numerical prediction error; the stated limitation is qualitative.
rows.check: Table 7 reports strategy success rates, not prediction errors. The authors only assert that large-K predictions are less precise, and at K=500 the All strategy drops ~10%, which they attribute to saturation and noise. The numbers_found value '1/1' is meaningless. The row is better read as qualitative.

relationships.condition: Real-world π0 fine-tuning, Mouse in Drawer and Fold Towel – Spatial, small extrapolation range
relationships.reason: The authors report that fitted power-law curves predicted added-data success almost exactly (r1, r2). This is figure-only and qualitative.
relationships.display_finding: Fitted power-law curves predicted added-data success almost exactly over the small extrapolation range.

relationships.condition: Noisy real evaluations (Fold Towel – Visual) and large data budgets (Peg Insertion – Spatial, K up to 500)
relationships.reason: An outlier distorts one fit (r3). The authors state large-K predictions are less precise amid saturation and noise (r4).
relationships.display_finding: An outlier distorted one fit, while saturation and noise reduced prediction precision at large data budgets up to K = 500.
